concepts.title: Failure of Point Prediction: Multimodal Distributions
concepts.one_liner: Point prediction methods like least-squares regression fail when the true data distribution is multimodal, often resulting in predictions that have zero probability.
concepts.content:
Least-squares regression fits a function $f: \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \mathcal{Y}$ to produce a single point prediction $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$. This approach fails when a problem is fundamentally ambiguous, such as colorizing a grayscale image where multiple valid colors may exist for a single input.

(see figure: Different kinds of predictive distributions.)

In a bimodal case where a shirt could be teal or pink, least-squares regression predicts the mean of the distribution—a gray color. This prediction is entirely wrong because it has zero probability under the true data distribution. While using different loss functions like $L_1$ might change the result, a single point prediction can only ever represent one mode. 

To improve results, we can predict a distribution $p_{\theta}(A \mid l)$. A Gaussian distribution captures variance but remains unimodal. More expressive options include a mixture of Gaussians or a categorical distribution ($\texttt{Cat}$). Categorical distributions are particularly powerful because they can represent any number of modes up to the resolution of the quantized data. Softmax regression is a common application of this, modeling a maximally expressive predictive distribution over a quantized decision space.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard regression models often fail in real-world scenarios where one input can lead to multiple valid outputs. Understanding the failure of point prediction motivates the shift toward probabilistic and generative modeling to capture the full range of possibilities.
concepts.recap_md: - Point predictions like the mean of a distribution can result in impossible values in multimodal data.

key_passage.text: Because the true distribution has two equally probable modes, and a single point prediction can only ever represent one mode.

concepts.title: Limitations of Classification for Prediction
concepts.one_liner: While classification handles multimodality, it suffers from quantization error and an exponential explosion in the number of classes for high-dimensional data.
concepts.content:
Classification addresses some deficiencies of point prediction but introduces new challenges: quantization error and the curse of dimensionality. 

Quantization error occurs because continuous values must be binned into discrete classes. While increasing the number of classes $k$ can reduce this error (e.g., using $k=256$ for 8-bit image channels), the second issue is more severe. To predict the color values of $N$ pixels with resolution $k$ requires $k^{2N}$ classes. For a standard $256 \times 256$ image, the number of classes required becomes astronomically large, making grid-based quantization unscalable for high-dimensional outputs.

(see figure: The funny shape of the $lab$ color gamut is because not every $ab$ value maps to a valid pixel color. When working with predictions over $lab$ color space, we may map $ab$ values that fall outside...)
concepts.motivation_md: Using classification for continuous prediction tasks (like image generation) seems like a good way to handle multiple modes, but the computational cost scales poorly as the output size increases.

concepts.title: Failure of Independent Predictions: Joint Structure
concepts.one_liner: Independent pixel predictions fail to capture joint structure, leading to inconsistent or 'flipped' results in ambiguous regions.
concepts.content:
To avoid the curse of dimensionality, models often factorize the joint distribution by making independent predictions for each pixel: $p_{\theta}(\mathbf{ab} \mid \mathbf{l}) = \prod_{n=1}^N\prod_{m=1}^M p_{\theta}(ab[n,m,:] \mid \mathbf{l})$. This assumes conditional independence: each pixel's color is independent of others given the input luminance. 

This assumption is implicit in any multidimensional least-squares ($L_2$) regression. Because the $L_2$ loss factorizes as a product over pairwise potentials, the Hammersley-Clifford theorem implies the model treats all output dimensions as independent given the input. 

This 'unstructured prediction' causes significant problems in ambiguous cases. For instance, if a model is unsure if a shirt is teal or pink, slight changes in input luminance can cause the per-pixel classifier to flip between the two colors. This results in chaotic, inconsistent color transitions across the image.

(see figure: Color flipping can arise from a smooth underlying predictive distribution, on top of which independent choices are made.)

[FIGURE:b268dfef8da91f88 | A real example of color flipping from @zhang2016colorful.]
concepts.motivation_md: In many real-world tasks like image colorization, pixels are not independent; they must form a coherent object. If a model treats them independently, the resulting output will likely be noisy and physically impossible.
concepts.recap_md: - Unstructured prediction assumes each output dimension is independent given the input.

key_passage.text: The underlying assumption of this factorization is one of conditional independence: each pixel's ab value is considered to be conditionally independent from all other pixels' ab values, given the observed luminance (of all pixels).

motivation.text: So, whether you are using per-pixel classification, or least-squares regression, you are implicitly fitting a model that assumes independence between all the output pixels, conditioned on the input. This causes problems.

concepts.title: Conditional Generative Models

position.section_title: Conditional Generative Models Solve Multimodal Structured Prediction

concepts.one_liner: Conditional generative models are structured prediction methods that model multimodal distributions and joint dependencies in the output space.
concepts.content:
Conditional generative models are a general family of prediction methods designed to overcome the limitations of standard approaches in computer vision. They achieve this by modeling a multimodal distribution of predictions and modeling joint structure. 

These models are considered structured prediction methods because they do not factorize the output into independent potentials conditioned on the input. Instead, conditional generative modeling captures a full distribution of possibilities over the joint configuration of outputs.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard models fail when there are multiple right answers or when parts of the output must be consistent with each other. Conditional generative models solve both problems simultaneously.
concepts.recap_md: - These models handle multimodality by representing a full distribution of possible outputs.

concepts.title: CycleGAN
concepts.one_liner: CycleGAN is a generative model that translates between two domains using a cycle-consistent objective to ensure mappings are reversible and realistic.
concepts.content:
Adding the cycle-consistency loss to the conditional generative model learning problem yields the complete CycleGAN objective: 

$$ 
\begin{aligned} 
    \arg\min_{\theta,\psi}\max_{\phi} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}} \big[ \log d_{\phi}^{Y}(g_{	heta}(\mathbf{x})) + \log (1 - d_{\phi}^{Y}(\mathbf{y})) + \left\lVert\mathbf{x} - f_{\psi}(g_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}))\right\rVert_1 + \\ 
    \log d_{\phi}^{X}(f_{\psi}(\mathbf{y})) + \log (1 - d_{\phi}^{X}(\mathbf{x})) + \left\lVert\mathbf{y} - g_{\theta}(f_{\psi}(\mathbf{y}))\right\rVert_1 \big] 
\end{aligned} 
$$ 

This model translates from domain $X$ to domain $Y$ and back, such that the outputs in domain $Y$ look realistic according to a domain $Y$ discriminator, and vice versa for domain $X$. The mappings are cycle-consistent: one complete cycle from $X$ to $Y$ and back should arrive where it started (and vice versa). (see figure: CycleGAN schematic. Figure derived from @CycleGAN2017)
concepts.motivation_md: CycleGAN allows for image-to-image translation between two domains without requiring paired training examples, relying instead on the assumption that the mapping should be reversible.

concepts.title: Limitations of Cycle-Consistency
concepts.one_liner: Cycle-consistency encourages one-to-one mappings but can be confounded by permutations that satisfy the objective while producing incorrect results.
concepts.content: The cycle-consistency losses encourage that the translation is a one-to-one function, and thereby reduce the number of valid solutions. This is a good idea when the true solution is indeed one-to-one, as is often the case in translation problems. However, other symmetries still exist and may confound methods like CycleGAN: if we permute the correct $X$-to-$Y$ mapping and apply the inverse permutation to the $Y$-to-$X$ mapping, then CycleGAN will still be satisfied but the mapping will now be incorrect.
concepts.motivation_md: While cycle-consistency constrains the search space for mappings, it is important to understand its failure modes, such as when the model learns a consistent but semantically incorrect permutation.

concepts.title: Trend toward General-Purpose Modeling
concepts.one_liner: A current trend in artificial intelligence is replacing bespoke, task-specific systems with general-purpose conditional generative models.
concepts.content: Many problems in vision can be phrased as structured prediction, and conditional generative models are a great approach to these problems. They provide a unified and simple solution to a diverse array of problems. A current trend in computer vision (and all of artificial intelligence) is to replace bespoke systems for specific kinds of structured prediction—object detectors, image captioning systems, and so on—with general-purpose conditional generative models. This trend toward general-purpose modeling tools is why modern study focuses less on special-purpose systems for specific vision problems.
concepts.motivation_md: General-purpose models simplify the AI landscape by providing a single framework capable of solving many different tasks that were previously handled by specialized architectures.

concepts.title: Amortized Inference

position.section_title: Conditional Generative Models Solve Multimodal Structured Prediction

concepts.one_liner: Amortized inference is a technique where a model learns a direct mapping from inputs to outputs through a neural network to approximate the results of iterative inference algorithms.
concepts.content: Amortized inference refers to a "thinking fast" approach to prediction where inference is performed through a single forward pass of a neural network. This contrasts with models like conditional random fields (CRFs) that "think slow" by running iterative algorithms such as belief propagation for each query. In amortized inference, the computational cost of inference is amortized over a training phase. This phase learns a direct mapping from inputs to outputs that approximates the solution that would have been obtained through exact inference on that input.
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional probabilistic models often require expensive iterative algorithms to make predictions at test time. Amortized inference solves this by shifting the computational burden to the training phase, allowing for nearly instantaneous predictions during deployment by using a neural network to approximate the inference process.
concepts.recap_md: - It replaces iterative inference algorithms with a single forward pass of a neural network.

concepts.title: Conditional Generative Adversarial Networks

position.section_title: A Tour of Popular Conditional Models

concepts.one_liner: Conditional Generative Adversarial Networks extend GANs by providing conditioning information to both the generator and the discriminator to model specific conditional distributions.
concepts.content: A generative adversarial network (GAN) can be made conditional by adding $\mathbf{x}$ as an input to both the generator and the discriminator: $$\begin{aligned} \arg\min_{\theta}\max_{\phi} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z},\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}} \big[ \log d_{\phi}(\mathbf{x}, g_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z})) + \log (1 - d_{\phi}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y})) \big] \end{aligned}$$ This modification changes the discriminator's task from identifying real versus synthetic outputs to identifying real versus synthetic input-output pairs. An input-output pair is considered synthetic if the output looks synthetic or if the output does not match the input. If both issues are avoided, the produced samples are $iid$ with respect to the true conditional distribution of the data $p_{\texttt{data}}(Y \bigm | \mathbf{x})$.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard GANs generate samples from a general distribution but offer no control over the specific characteristics of the output. Conditional GANs allow users to direct the generation process by providing specific input data, enabling tasks like generating an image from a specific class or label.
concepts.recap_md: - The discriminator evaluates the validity of the input-output pair $(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y})$ rather than just the output.

What this does is change the job of the discriminator from asking "is the output real or synthetic?" to asking "is the input-output *pair* real or synthetic?"

A conditional variational autoencoder (cVAE) defines a conditional distribution as the marginal over a latent variable: $$\begin{aligned} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{y} \bigm | \mathbf{x}) = \int_{\mathbf{z}} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{y} \bigm | \mathbf{z}, \mathbf{x})p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z} \bigm | \mathbf{x})d\mathbf{z} \end{aligned}$$ In cVAEs, we restrict attention to latent variables $\mathbf{z}$ that are independent of the inputs $\mathbf{x}$, resulting in the likelihood model: $$\begin{aligned} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{y} \bigm | \mathbf{x}) = \int_{\mathbf{z}} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{y} \bigm | \mathbf{z}, \mathbf{x})p_{\mathbf{z}}(\mathbf{z})d\mathbf{z} \end{aligned}$$ This corresponds to the following graphical model:
[FIGURE:184e45370a8359cb]

The latent variable $\mathbf{z}$ should encode information about $\mathbf{y}$ that is independent of what $\mathbf{x}$ already provides. For example, if predicting the next frame $\mathbf{y}$ of a bouncing ball from a frame $\mathbf{x}$, $\mathbf{x}$ provides color and position, while $\mathbf{z}$ might capture the unknown velocity. Marginalizing over $\mathbf{z}$ allows the model to place maximum likelihood on the data. (see figure: A scenario where a yellow ball is moving across a plane. The observation, $\mathbf{x}$, is a static frame. From that observation, we know what will be the color and rough position of the ball in the...)

Like regular VAEs, cVAEs use an encoder to predict the importance sampling distribution $p_{\theta}(Z \bigm | \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y})$. During training, both the encoder and decoder take the conditioning information $\mathbf{x}$ as input. (see figure: cVAE architecture. The dotted lines indicate that the *target encoder* is only used during training; at test time, usage follows the solid path.)
concepts.motivation_md: Standard VAEs learn to represent data in a latent space but cannot easily generate data conditioned on specific external information. cVAEs allow for structured generation where the model uses the conditioning input to handle known features and the latent space to handle remaining uncertainty.

concepts.title: Conditional Autoregressive Models

position.section_title: A Tour of Popular Conditional Models

concepts.one_liner: Conditional autoregressive models treat conditioning inputs as a prefix to the sequence being modeled, factorizing the probability into a series of conditional predictions.
concepts.content: Autoregressive models naturally model sequences of conditional distributions. To condition them on inputs $\mathbf{x}$, we can concatenate $\mathbf{x}$ as a prefix to the sequence of $y$ values, creating the sequence $[x_1, \ldots, x_m, y_1, \ldots, y_n]$. The probability model factorizes as: $$\begin{aligned} p_{\theta}(\mathbf{y} \bigm | \mathbf{x}) &= \prod_{i=1}^n p_{\theta}(y_i \bigm | y_1, \ldots, y_{i-1}, x_1, \ldots, x_m) \end{aligned}$$ Each term in the product predicts the next item given all previous items, including the conditioning prefix. Because this structure is identical to unconditional autoregressive modeling, the same implementation and tools can be used for both cases, simply by choosing whether or not to prefix the sequence.
concepts.motivation_md: Autoregressive models are powerful for sequence generation but need a way to incorporate context. By treating the context as a prefix, we can leverage existing sequence modeling architectures to generate outputs that are consistent with given constraints or history.
concepts.recap_md: - Conditioning is achieved by prefixing the target sequence with the conditioning variables $\mathbf{x}$.

motivation.text: Each distribution in this product is a prediction of the next item in a sequence given the previous items, which is no different than what we had for unconditional autoregressive models. Therefore, the tools for modeling unconditional autoregressive distributions are also appropriate for modeling conditional autoregressive distributions.

concepts.title: Conditional Diffusion Models

position.section_title: A Tour of Popular Conditional Models

concepts.one_liner: Conditional diffusion models incorporate conditioning variables into the denoising function to guide the generative process toward specific outputs.
concepts.content: Diffusion models can be made conditional by concatenating the conditioning variables $\mathbf{x}$ into the input of the denoising function: $$\begin{aligned} \hat{\mathbf{y}}_{t-1} = f_{\theta}(\mathbf{y}_t, t, \mathbf{x}) \end{aligned}$$ Both diffusion and autoregressive models convert generative modeling into a sequence of supervised prediction problems. Conditioning is achieved by augmenting the training pairs from $\{\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \mathbf{y}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$ to $\{[\mathbf{x}^{(i)}, \mathbf{c}^{(i)}], \mathbf{y}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^N$, where $\mathbf{c}$ represents additional paired observations. For example, in text-to-image synthesis, providing a text description as an additional input to $f_{\theta}$ allows the model to denoise toward an image that matches that text. (see figure: Text-conditional diffusion model.)
concepts.motivation_md: Unconditional diffusion models generate high-quality but random samples. By adding conditioning variables like text or class labels to the denoising step, we can steer the model to generate specific content that satisfies user-provided constraints.
concepts.recap_md: - Conditioning is implemented by adding the variable $\mathbf{x}$ as an input to the denoising function $f_{\theta}$.

key_passage.text: All we need to do is concatenate the conditioning variables, $\mathbf{x}$, into the input to the denoising function: $\hat{\mathbf{y}}_{t-1} = f_{\theta}(\mathbf{y}_t, t, \mathbf{x})$

motivation.text: The intuition is that if we give $f_{\theta}$ a description of the image as an additional input, then it can do a better job at solving its prediction task. Because of this, $f_{\theta}$ will become sensitive to the text command, and if you give different text it will denoise toward a different image---an image that matches that text!

concepts.title: Image-to-Image Translation
concepts.one_liner: Image-to-image translation is the task of mapping an input image from one representation or domain to another, such as converting a sketch into a photograph.
concepts.content: Image-to-image problems are mapping tasks where both the input and output are images, defined as arrays of size $N \times M \times C$ (height by width by channels). These problems are common in computer vision and include tasks such as colorization, next frame prediction, depth map estimation, and semantic segmentation. This perspective treats these tasks as translating from one view of the data to another; for instance, semantic segmentation translates a color-based view of the world into a semantic-based view. The goal of image-to-image translation is to learn these mappings, such as translating from pixels to semantics or from a photograph to a painting.
concepts.motivation_md: Many computer vision tasks share a common structure: they require transforming an input image into a different but spatially aligned output image. Defining these as 'translation' allows for a unified framework to solve diverse problems like segmentation, colorization, and style transfer.
concepts.recap_md: - It involves mapping an input image to an output image of the same or similar spatial dimensions.

key_passage.text: Image-to-image problems are mapping problems where the input is an image and the output is also an image, where we will here think of an image as any array of size N × M × C (height by width by number of channels). This perspective yields the problem of image-to-image translation; just like we can translate from English to French, can we translate from pixels to semantics, or perhaps from a photographic depiction of scene to a painting of that same scene?

concepts.title: Image-to-Image Translation with a Conditional GAN
concepts.one_liner: The pix2pix method uses a conditional GAN with a U-Net generator and a CNN discriminator to perform image-to-image translation.
concepts.content: One approach to image-to-image translation is using a conditional GAN, as popularized by the "pix2pix" paper. In this framework, the generator maps an input image (such as a facade layout map) to an output image (such as a matching photo). The generator typically uses an image-to-image architecture like a U-Net, which is a CNN with accordion-shaped skip connections. The discriminator is a regular CNN that maps the output image to a scalar score representing whether the input-output pair is real or synthetic. (see figure: The pix2pix @pix2pix2017 model applied to translating a facade layout map into a photo of the facade. The model was trained on the CMP Facades Database @Tylecek13 and the input and ground truth...)
concepts.motivation_md: Standard supervised learning for image translation often results in blurry outputs because simple loss functions like MSE average over possible outcomes. Using a GAN loss forces the model to produce sharp, realistic images that are indistinguishable from real data.
concepts.recap_md: - It utilizes a U-Net architecture for the generator to preserve spatial information through skip connections.

concepts.title: Omitting Noise in Conditional GANs
concepts.one_liner: In some conditional GAN implementations, the noise input is omitted because the input image provides sufficient entropy for the generator.
concepts.content: In certain conditional GAN settings, noise inputs are omitted, and the generator takes only the image $\mathbf{x}$ as input. This is done because the input image $\mathbf{x}$ often contains enough entropy by itself, making additional noise unnecessary for creating variety in the model's outputs. However, the downside to this approach is that the model becomes deterministic, providing only one prediction $\mathbf{y}$ for each input $\mathbf{x}$.
concepts.motivation_md: While GANs are theoretically designed to map noise to data, in conditional tasks like image-to-image translation, the network often learns to ignore the noise. Omitting it simplifies the architecture when a single high-quality mapping is preferred over a variety of outputs.
concepts.recap_md: - The generator relies on the entropy of the input image $\mathbf{x}$ instead of an explicit noise vector.

This is because the input image $\mathbf{x}$ has enough entropy by itself, and you don't necessarily need additional noise to create variety in the outputs of the model.

concepts.title: Conditional GAN as a Learned Loss Function
concepts.one_liner: A conditional GAN can be viewed as a regression problem where the discriminator acts as a learned loss function that adapts to the data structure and generator behavior.
concepts.content: One way to think about this setup is that it is a regression problem with a *learned loss function* $d_{\phi}$, a view shown in (see figure: The discriminator of a GAN as a learned loss function.). This loss function adapts to the structure of the data and the behavior of the generator to penalize just the relevant errors the generator is currently making. It can help to also add a conventional regression loss, such as the $L_1$ loss, to stabilize the optimization process, yielding the following objective: $$\begin{aligned} \arg\min_G\max_D \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z},\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}} \big[ \log d_{\phi}(\mathbf{x}, g_{\theta}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z})) + \log (1 - d_{\phi}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y})) + \left\lVert g_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) - \mathbf{y}\right\rVert_1 \big] \end{aligned}$$
concepts.motivation_md: Traditional loss functions like L1 or L2 often fail to capture complex data structures in image-to-image tasks. Using a GAN discriminator as a learned loss allows the model to adaptively penalize errors based on the data's underlying distribution.

concepts.title: PatchGAN Discriminator
concepts.one_liner: The PatchGAN is a discriminator architecture that scores individual image patches as real or fake and averages these scores to determine the total loss.
concepts.content: One popular architecture for image-to-image tasks is a **PatchGAN** discriminator, in which we score each *patch* in the output image as real or fake and take the average over patch scores as our total loss: $$\begin{aligned} d_{\phi}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = \frac{1}{NM} \sum_{i=0}^N \sum_{j=0}^M d_{\phi}^{\texttt{patch}}(\mathbf{x}[i:i+k,j:j+k], \mathbf{y}[i:i+k,j:j+k]) \end{aligned}$$ where $k \times k$ is the patch size. This operation is equivalent to the sliding window action of a CNN, so $d_{\phi}^{\texttt{patch}}$ can simply be implemented as a CNN that outputs a $2 \times N \times M$ feature map of real-versus-synthetic scores. Naturally, patches can be sampled at different strides and resolutions, depending on the exact architecture of the CNN $d_{\phi}^{\texttt{patch}}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard discriminators that score an entire image can be difficult to train and require many parameters. PatchGAN focuses on local structure, making the learning task more manageable and statistically efficient.

concepts.title: Analysis of PatchGAN Patch Sizes
concepts.one_liner: PatchGAN discriminators offer statistical advantages by using fewer parameters on more data, though their effectiveness depends heavily on the chosen patch size.
concepts.content: The PatchGAN strategy has two advantages over scoring the whole image: it can be easier to model if a patch is real or synthetic ($d_{\phi}^{\texttt{patch}}$ needs fewer parameters), and there are more patches in the training data than there are images. These properties give PatchGAN discriminators a statistical advantage. The disadvantage is that the PatchGAN only has the capacity to penalize errors observable within a single patch, as shown in (see figure: Varying the receptive field (patch size) of the convolutional discriminator affects what kinds of structure the discriminator enforces. These results are from @pix2pix2017). A $1\times1$ discriminator cannot penalize errors in joint pixel statistics like edge structure, resulting in blurry results. Larger receptive fields enforce higher order patch realism but cannot model structure larger than the patch size, potentially causing tiling artifacts. Quality may degrade with very large discriminators (e.g., $286\times286$) because the task becomes too hard given limited training data.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the trade-offs of patch sizes helps in designing discriminators that balance local detail with global structure while remaining computationally and statistically efficient.

Larger receptive fields can enforce higher order patch realism, but cannot model structure larger than the patch size (hence the tiling artifacts that are occur with a period roughly equal to the patch size).

concepts.title: Unpaired Image-to-Image Translation
concepts.one_liner: Unpaired image-to-image translation is the task of learning to map between two domains without direct correspondence between specific training instances.
concepts.content: In many settings, paired training data $\{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}\}$ is hard to obtain. For example, translating a photo into a Cezanne painting (see figure: A style transfer example from the CycleGAN paper @CycleGAN2017 *Input photo source*: Alexei A. Efros.) would require the artist to paint specific scenes for our training set. However, humans can imagine these changes because we understand the general style of the target domain without needing exact pairs. This is the **unpaired translation** setting, distinguished from **paired translation** as shown in (see figure: (left) An example of paired image-to-image translation (colorization) versus (right) unpaired translation (photo to Cezanne). concepts.title: Emergent Pairing in GANs
concepts.one_liner: In GANs, the specific mapping between input noise and output data is not predetermined but emerges during training to satisfy the objective of matching the data distribution.
concepts.content: GANs train a mapping from a noise distribution to a data distribution $p(Z) \rightarrow p(X)$. They do this without knowing the pairing between $\mathbf{z}$ and $\mathbf{x}$ values in the training data. Instead this pairing is *emergent*. Which $\mathbf{z}$-vector corresponds to which $\mathbf{x}$ is not predetermined but self-organizes to satisfy the GAN objective: all $\mathbf{z}$-vectors should map to realistic images, and, collectively they should map to the data distribution.
concepts.motivation_md: This self-organizing property is what allows GANs to be applied to problems where explicit supervision of individual correspondences is unavailable.

concepts.title: Symmetries in Unpaired Learning
concepts.one_liner: Unpaired learning problems contain many symmetries where different mappings achieve the same loss because the GAN objective only evaluates the output distribution, not individual instance matches.
concepts.content: A GAN may learn the correct mapping from $\mathbf{x}$ to $\mathbf{y}$, but there are many symmetries in this learning problem where different mappings achieve equivalent loss. For example, any permutation in the mapping does not affect the output *distribution*, and the GAN objective only cares about the output distribution. Put another away, the GAN discriminator is different than a normal loss function. Rather than checking if the output matches a target *instance* (that $g_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}^{(i)})$ matches $\mathbf{y}^{(i)}$), it checks if the output is part of an admissible set of realistic $\mathbf{y}$ values. This property makes GANs perfect for working with unpaired data, where we don't have instance-level supervision but only have set-level supervision.
concepts.motivation_md: Recognizing that standard GAN losses only enforce distribution matching explains why additional constraints are needed to ensure the learned mapping is meaningful and not just a random permutation.
concepts.recap_md: - The GAN objective is satisfied as long as the set of generated outputs matches the target distribution.

concepts.title: Unpaired Learning
concepts.one_liner: Unpaired learning uses labels to identify which set a datapoint belongs to, providing set-level supervision rather than instance-level correspondence.
concepts.content: We call this **unpaired** learning rather than **unsupervised** because we still have supervision in the form of labels indicating which *set* each datapoint belongs to. That is, we know whether each image is an $\mathbf{x}$ or a $\mathbf{y}$.

concepts.title: Cycle-Consistency
concepts.one_liner: Cycle-consistency is a constraint requiring that a sample translated from one domain to another and back again should return to its original state.
concepts.content: A regular GAN objective for mapping $X$ to $Y$ does not distinguish between the correct mapping and others that achieve the same output distribution. To break the symmetry we need to add additional constraints like **cycle-consistency**. The idea is that if we translate from $X$ to $Y$ and then back to $X$, we should arrive where we started. In natural language processing, this is known as **backtranslation**. Cycle-consistency losses are regularizers that encourage a learned mapping to be roughly one-to-one. The cycle-consistency losses from CycleGAN are: $$ \begin{aligned} \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{cyc}}(\mathbf{x};g_{\theta},f_{\psi}) &= \left\lVert\mathbf{x} - f_{\psi}(g_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}))\right\rVert_1\\ \mathcal{L}_{\texttt{cyc}}(\mathbf{y};g_{\theta},f_{\psi}) &= \left\lVert\mathbf{y} - g_{\theta}(f_{\psi}(\mathbf{y}))\right\rVert_1 \end{aligned} $$
concepts.motivation_md: Without cycle-consistency, unpaired translation models can learn arbitrary mappings that satisfy the discriminator but lose the content of the input. This constraint ensures the mapping is reversible and preserves information.
concepts.recap_md: - Cycle-consistency requires that $f(g(x)) \approx x$ and $g(f(y)) \approx y$.
